description: MMMU (Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning) is a benchmark of 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines (Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering) across 30 subjects and 183 subfields. It features 30 highly heterogeneous image types and interleaved text-image inputs, designed to evaluate expert-level perception and reasoning with domain-specific knowledge in large multimodal models.
name: MMMU
publisher: MMMU (University of Waterloo, The Ohio State University, IN.AI Research)
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students (including co-authors) specializing in the relevant academic majors across 30 subjects. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent a wide range of experts in the corresponding 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human expert performance was measured on the validation set: 90 college senior students (3 per subject) completed 900 validation questions. Expert accuracy ranged from 76.2% (worst) to 88.6% (best), with a median of 82.6%. An error analysis was conducted on 150 randomly sampled GPT-4V error cases, categorized by expert annotators into: Perceptual Error (35%), Lack of Knowledge (29%), Reasoning Error (26%), Textual Understanding Error (4%), Rejection to Answer (3%), Annotation Error (2%), and Answer Extraction Error (1%).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Over 50 university students specializing in the relevant majors were recruited as annotators. They collected multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, and created new questions based on their expertise where necessary. Annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoid data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution, and select questions without immediately available answers to mitigate data contamination. A detailed annotation protocol is provided in Appendix A (covering data collection, general guidelines, data format and structure, quality control and validation, handling ambiguities, ethical considerations, data contamination considerations, and example questions).
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges that the manual curation process may carry biases. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. Additionally, annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers to mitigate data contamination concerns from foundation models. The benchmark excludes subjects like law and linguistics where it was difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were manually collected by a team of over 50 college students (including co-authors) from various disciplines and subjects, drawing from online sources, textbooks, and lecture materials. The collection process involved three stages: (1) selecting 30 subjects from six disciplines based on the principle that visual inputs should be commonly adopted; (2) recruiting university students specializing in these majors to collect multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary; (3) annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations and to select questions without immediately available answers to avoid data contamination.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Multimodal questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, and online resources across 30 subjects and 6 disciplines. The raw collection resulted in approximately 13K questions from various sources before quality filtering.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI, as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and "90th percentile of skilled adults," nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle. The manual curation process may carry biases, and the focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. The benchmark excludes some subjects (e.g., law, linguistics) where it was difficult to find enough relevant multimodal problems.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Two-step data cleaning was performed: (1) lexical overlap and source URL similarity were used to identify potential duplicate problems, which were then reviewed by authors to eliminate duplications; (2) problems were distributed among co-authors for format and typo checking to ensure adherence to a standardized format. In a third stage, problems were categorized into four difficulty levels (very easy, easy, medium, hard), and approximately 10% classified as very easy were excluded from the benchmark.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is designed to monitor progress towards Expert AGI, defined as AI systems reaching "at least 90th percentile of skilled adults" in a broad range of tasks. Achieving Expert AGI could lead to significant risks of job displacement and economic disruption, as it marks "the substitution threshold for machine intelligence in lieu of human labor" for many industries. The paper frames MMMU as a necessary (though not sufficient) criterion for Expert AGI systems.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating multimodal foundation models on expert-level, college-level multi-discipline tasks requiring domain-specific knowledge and deliberate reasoning. Intended to stimulate the community to build next-generation multimodal foundation models towards expert artificial general intelligence, and to monitor progress towards Expert AGI.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a fixed number of independent annotations per item; questions were collected and reviewed but no per-item annotation count is given.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: No specific timeframe (start/end dates) for data collection is mentioned in the paper.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not discuss missing data handling in the collection process.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; the dataset consists of discrete questions and images with no missing value imputation needed.
null_reasons.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: No post-collection data manipulation, augmentation, or resampling is described for the dataset itself.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No explicit versioning or maintenance plan is described beyond the live-updating leaderboard.
null_reasons.rai:machineAnnotationTools: No machine annotation tools were used in the dataset creation process; annotation was done manually by human experts.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: The evidence quote only says annotators were recruited university students; it does not name a specific annotation platform. The value I extracted goes beyond what the evidence supports.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The evidence quote cited does not actually discuss personal or sensitive information in the dataset. The paper does not explicitly discuss PII or sensitive data handling; the medical images are from textbooks/educational materials but this is not stated in the quoted evidence.

evidence.name: We introduce MMMU : a new benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning.
evidence.description: MMMU includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types, such as charts, diagrams, maps, tables, music sheets, and chemical structures.
